ingredients.name: Freshly grated coconut
ingredients.notes: about 3 cups; unsweetened desiccated coconut soaked in 1/4 cup warm water can substitute

ingredients.name: Kithul jaggery
ingredients.notes: grated or crumbled; brown sugar or palm sugar can substitute, though colour will be lighter

ingredients.name: Kithul treacle
ingredients.notes: 1/4 cup; for dissolving the jaggery and darkening the colour

ingredients.name: Fine semolina
ingredients.notes: about 1/2 cup; dry-roasted in a pan until lightly golden before use

ingredients.name: All-purpose flour
ingredients.notes: about 2/3 cup, sifted with the baking powder

ingredients.name: Cashew nuts
ingredients.notes: coarsely chopped, plus a few halves for the top

ingredients.name: Egg
ingredients.notes: separated; white and yolk beaten separately. Traditional recipes use no egg; the modern version with egg is softer.

steps.instruction: Preheat the oven to 160C (325F). Line an 8-inch (20cm) square baking tin with parchment paper and grease well.
Dry-roast the semolina in a pan over low heat, stirring constantly, until it is lightly golden and smells nutty -- about 5-7 minutes. Set aside to cool.
Dry-roast the fennel seeds, cardamom pods, and cloves separately in a dry pan for 2 minutes until fragrant. Cool, remove cardamom shells, and crush/grind to a coarse powder.

In a pot, dissolve the jaggery in the water and treacle over medium heat, stirring until fully dissolved. Add the grated coconut and cook together for 3-5 minutes, stirring, until the mixture thickens slightly. Remove from heat and cool for 10 minutes.
Once the coconut-jaggery mixture has cooled to warm (not hot), stir in the roasted semolina, chopped dates, chopped cashews, ground spices, cinnamon, and salt. Mix well.
If using egg: beat the yolk and stir into the mixture. In a separate bowl, beat the egg white to soft peaks and fold in gently. If omitting egg (traditional method): proceed to the next step.
Sift in the flour mixed with a pinch of baking powder and fold through until just combined. Do not overmix.

Pour into the prepared tin and spread evenly. Arrange cashew halves on top. Bake at 160C for 50-60 minutes until a skewer comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached (not wet batter). The top should be deep golden brown.
Cool completely in the tin before cutting into squares. Bibikkan improves in flavour over the next 1-2 days and keeps well in an airtight container for up to 2 weeks.

source_site: tasty.co, cross-checked against rasakama.wordpress.com, bigoven.com, foodhow.com, gzrecipes.com, cuisinesofworld.com, bakerrecipes.com, and Wikipedia (Bibikkan)
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 8+ independent sources; moderate trust score reflects genuine disagreement between traditional (no egg, no baking powder, no flour) and modern versions
notes: Bibikkan is a dark, moist, dense coconut-and-jaggery cake with a distinctive chewy-fudgy interior and a long keeping quality, eaten especially at New Year and other celebrations. Sources diverge meaningfully on whether to use egg and baking powder (modern, lighter version) or omit them entirely (traditional, denser version) -- rasakama.wordpress.com explicitly states that adding egg and baking powder creates 'modern coconut cake', not traditional bibikkan. This entry represents a practical middle ground; to make the traditional version simply omit the egg and flour entirely and bake slightly longer. Winter melon preserve (puhul dosi) and preserved ginger are common optional additions that add extra complexity; they are omitted here for simplicity but noted as authentic additions. The dark colour comes from the jaggery and treacle -- if the jaggery you have is light-coloured, some sources recommend making a small sugar caramel to deepen the colour before adding other ingredients.
